newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S. wants sweeter Colombian investment terms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wants sweeter Colombian investment terms.

text.p: U.S. ambassador Myles Frechette delivered an aggressive free trade message and a thinly veiled demand to sweeten terms for American investors when he met Colombia's business leaders on Friday.

He told Colombian Foreign Trade Minister Morris Harf that U.S. investors were keenly eyeing sectors of the Colombian economy soon to be thrown open to greater competition but called for more lucrative terms for foreign companies in other sectors, particularly the key oil industry.

As on previous occasions, Frechette linked trade relations to U.S. demands for stiffer measures against narcotics trafficking and said that economic sanctions against Colombia were under consideration for what the Clinton administration believes is President Ernesto Samper's failure to crack down hard enough on the drug cartels.

"The best way for Colombia to maintain growth and ensure free competition is to continue opening its economy to foreign investment. In my opinion the fewer obstacles to foreign investment the better. Let's hope that Colombia's private sector supports that," Frechette told the meeting at the headquarters of El Espectador newspaper.
The U.S. envoy was upbeat about the prospect of U.S. phone companies buying into Colombia when state-run Telecom loses its monopoly in the long distance and international market next year.
But echoing recent comments by British Petroleum (BP), he warned that the oil sector was still not lucrative enough for U.S. oil concerns.

"U.S. oil companies do not think the current contracts are sufficient to generate their interest. But changes could make Colombia more attractive and would be beneficial to its economy. We hope for good cooperation on energy matters," Frechette said.

Last week Jose Fernando Isaza, a veteran board member of the state-run oil company Ecopetrol resigned in protest at what he described as undue pressure to change BP's association contract for the Piedmonte project. Under a complex sliding-scale formula, Ecopetrol's share of the profits rises in line with production from between 50 percent to as much as 70 percent.
BP has objected that the project is not viable and Samper is studying the terms of the deal.

In response to businessmen's questions, Frechette denied the United States was looking to edge Samper out of the presidency but urged the private sector to use its political muscle to press Congress to rush through a package of tougher anti-drugs measures submitted by government in July.
